blocks.text: Everyone assumes you have to pay to park at Bondi. You don't — and this is the local secret I share with visiting friends every summer.

The spot is the residential streets north of Blair Street — that is, the blocks heading away from the beach. Punch "Blair Street" into your maps app, then simply head north (away from the water) and start looking. The parking here is free and unrestricted around the clock, no meters, no time limits.

On weekdays there are spaces until late afternoon, when residents start arriving home from work. On weekends it's busier, but the constant coming and going means you can usually snag something if you're patient — and much more easily if you're early.

From about 9am on a Saturday or Sunday, parking anywhere near Bondi becomes a genuine challenge. Beat the rush: get here early, grab a free spot north of Blair Street, and enjoy a quiet morning on the sand before the crowds roll in.

One caveat — always read the signs. As you get closer to the beach you'll hit timed and permit-only zones, so keep heading north until the restrictions drop off. For every other way to get to Bondi (train, bus, and the rest), see my full guide to parking and getting here.

items.q: Where is the free parking at Bondi Beach?
items.a: The residential streets north of Blair Street, heading away from the beach. It's free and unrestricted 24 hours, roughly a 5–7 minute walk to the sand.

items.q: What time should I arrive for a free spot?
items.a: Before 9am on weekends. Weekdays are easier until the late afternoon, when residents return home.

blocks.text: Bondi's Icebergs gets all the postcards, but if you ask me, Bronte Baths just down the coast is the more soulful swim. It's a saltwater pool carved straight into the sandstone at the southern end of Bronte Beach — free, unpretentious, and my favourite place for an early lap when I want to skip the crowds.

Bronte sits on the Eastern Beaches strip between Bondi to the north and Coogee to the south. The pool is cut into the rock shelf at the southern headland, so it fills and refreshes with the ocean — you're swimming in the sea, just with a wall between you and the swell. There's a shallower end that's good for kids, and it's a genuine lap-swimmer's pool the rest of the time.
Getting there

items: On foot — it's right on the Bondi to Coogee coastal walk, one of the best ways to arrive.
Public transport — train to Bondi Junction, then a bus down to Bronte. Easy and it skips the parking headache.
By car — there's parking around Bronte Road and the park, but it's limited and fills fast on a nice day, so come early.

blocks.title: Check before you go
blocks.text: Bronte Baths has been through staged upgrade works (over recent winters), and ocean pools are also periodically drained for cleaning — so it can be closed, especially in the cooler months. Check Waverley Council's ocean-pool status before you make a special trip.
Is it free? And can anyone use it?

Yes on both counts — Bronte Baths is completely free and open to the public, no entry fee. There are showers and changing facilities nearby (some may be coin-operated). It's an easygoing, welcoming spot for locals and visitors alike.

blocks.title: A word on the water
blocks.text: Bronte is a beautiful beach but a serious one — it's known for a strong permanent rip (the "Bronte Express"). The pool is calmer than the open beach, but conditions in and around it still change with the surf and tide. On the beach, swim between the red and yellow flags when lifeguards are patrolling, and check Beachsafe for current conditions.

items.q: Is Bronte Ocean Pool free?
items.a: Yes — Bronte Baths is completely free and open to the public. Showers and changing facilities nearby may be coin-operated.

items.q: Where is the Bronte Ocean Pool?
items.a: It's carved into the rock at the southern end of Bronte Beach, in Sydney's Eastern Suburbs, right on the Bondi to Coogee coastal walk.

items.q: Is the Bronte pool open all year?
items.a: It's generally open year-round in daylight hours, but it closes periodically for cleaning and has had staged upgrade works, mainly in winter. Check Waverley Council's ocean-pool status before a special trip.

blocks.text: Pack your bathers, walk a stretch of the coast to get there, and have a dip in one of Sydney's loveliest ocean pools. Bronte doesn't shout about itself — which is exactly why I love it.

blocks.text: If you're trying to picture the City2Surf course before race day, here's the route the way I'd talk you through it as a local — section by section, from the city start to the Bondi finish. For the official downloadable map with water stations and split points, head to city2surf.com.au; what follows is the lay of the land.
The course, section by section

items: Start — near Hyde Park, at Park and College Streets in the CBD, then a fast downhill along William Street.
Kings Cross — through the tunnel and out toward the harbour; this early stretch is quick, so don't get carried away.
Rose Bay — along New South Head Road beside the water. Enjoy it, because the hill is next.
Heartbreak Hill — an approximately 2 km climb from Rose Bay up to Vaucluse. This is the halfway point and the toughest part of the day.
Vaucluse to the coast — onto Old South Head Road and Military Road, with a few short sharp pinches before a rewarding downhill and big ocean views.
Bondi finish — a turnaround near Curlewis Street and roughly a final kilometre of flat switchback to the line on Queen Elizabeth Drive above the beach.

blocks.title: Reading the profile
blocks.text: The first few kilometres are net downhill and deceptively fast. The climbing is concentrated in the middle around Heartbreak Hill — and there are more little rises after it — so plan your effort to peak through the hills, not before them.
Best spots to watch or push hard

Rose Bay and the foot of Heartbreak Hill are my favourite places to spectate — the crowd support there genuinely carries runners up the climb. If you're racing, treat the top of the hill at Vaucluse as your cue to reassess your pace, and remember the sneaky final switchback at Bondi before you spend everything.

items.q: Where can I get the official City2Surf course map?
items.a: From the official site, city2surf.com.au, which publishes the current downloadable map with water stations, drink stations and split points.

items.q: Where does the City2Surf start and finish?
items.a: It starts near Hyde Park in the Sydney CBD (Park and College Streets) and finishes on Queen Elizabeth Drive above Bondi Beach, 14 km later.

items.q: How much of the course is uphill?
items.a: The signature climb is Heartbreak Hill, about 2 km from Rose Bay to Vaucluse near halfway, but there are also several shorter rises afterward before the downhill to Bondi.

blocks.text: "How cold is the water?" is the question I get asked most before someone's first Bondi swim. So here's my month-by-month rundown of what the sea usually does through the year. One handy thing to know: Bondi Icebergs isn't heated, so these figures double as a rough guide to the pool temperature too.

The numbers below are approximate long-term monthly averages — the actual water on any given day varies with currents, wind and the season, sometimes by a couple of degrees. For today's real reading, check the live water temperature in our daily Bondi weather & surf summary.
Bondi sea temperature, month by month

items: January — around 23°C. Peak summer swimming; warm and inviting.
February — around 23–24°C. Usually the warmest water of the year.
March — around 23°C. Still lovely, easing off as autumn nears.
April — around 21–22°C. Pleasant for most swimmers, cooler than the summer peak.
May — around 20°C. The cool-down begins; many switch to a wetsuit.
June — around 18–19°C. Winter setting in; better for surfers and hardy swimmers.
July — around 17–18°C. Typically the coldest of the year; wetsuit recommended.
August — around 17–18°C. A touch above July, but still properly cold.
September — around 18°C. Spring begins and the water slowly turns the corner.
October — around 19°C. Noticeably warmer; the regulars start coming back.
November — around 20–21°C. Building toward summer; increasingly comfortable.
December — around 22°C. Warm again — one of the best months to be in the water.

blocks.title: Warm air, cool water
blocks.text: Sydney's sea lags the seasons. Autumn water often feels warmer than you'd expect because it's still holding summer's heat, while spring can stay chilly even on a hot day. Don't judge the water by the air temperature.

items.q: What is the warmest month to swim at Bondi?
items.a: February, when the water averages around 23–24°C. January to March are all reliably warm.

items.q: How cold does Bondi get in winter?
items.a: The water bottoms out around 17–18°C in July and August. It's swimmable for the hardy, but most people wear a wetsuit from about May to September.

items.q: Is Bondi Icebergs pool heated?
items.a: No — Icebergs is an unheated ocean pool, so its temperature tracks the sea. These monthly averages are a good guide to what the pool will feel like.

blocks.text: Warm water or bracing winter dip, Bondi delivers something worth swimming for all year. Just pick your month — and maybe your wetsuit — to match.

blocks.text: People ask me this more than you'd think, usually with one eyebrow raised: are there snakes in Bondi? I always give the same answer — only one, and his name is Blake.

If you've wandered down Blair Street lately, you might have spotted a curious creature slithering along the footpath. Don't panic — this isn't the sort of snake that sends you running. He's the friendliest serpent in Sydney: Blake the Blair Street Snake, a community art project made entirely of painted rocks.

It starts with a single boulder — Blake's cheerful head, painted minty green with pink and black patches, perched beside a hand-lettered sign that reads: "I'm Blake the Blair St Snake. Add a painted rock to see how long I can get :)"

From there, a colourful line of rocks winds down the stone wall like scales on a giant, happy reptile. Some are splashed in pastels, others flecked with stars or faces, and a few were clearly painted by very small and very enthusiastic hands. Every week Blake stretches a little further as locals and passers-by add to him.
Why I love stumbling across Blake

In a world of "Do Not Touch" signs and endless screens, here's a simple invitation to join in. No permissions, no forms — just grab a rock, grab some paint, and make your mark. I've watched joggers pause mid-stride to admire him before carrying on toward the beach, and I've never once seen someone walk past without smiling.

Each rock tells a tiny story: maybe painted on a rainy afternoon, maybe made at a weekend craft session, maybe left by a visitor who wanted to be part of something local. To me, Blake is like Bondi's community diary — only instead of words, it's written in colour. Bondi's famous for its shimmering water and perfect surf, but this quirky reptile has become just as iconic in his own way.

If you're bringing kids, paint a rock at home the night before and let it dry — then it's ready to add to Blake's tail on the day. A weatherproof outdoor paint or a coat of clear sealer helps your rock survive Bondi's sun and salt air.

items.q: Are there actually dangerous snakes at Bondi Beach?
items.a: Bondi is a busy urban beach, so you're extremely unlikely to encounter a wild snake on the sand or promenade. The only "snake" locals talk about is Blake, the painted-rock art trail on Blair Street.

items.q: Where exactly is Blake the Blair Street Snake?
items.a: Along the stone wall on Blair Street in Bondi. Look for the minty-green painted boulder with the sign inviting you to add a rock — the trail of rocks grows from there.

items.q: Can I add my own rock?
items.a: Yes — that's the whole idea. Paint a rock, bring it down to Blair Street, and add it to the end of Blake's body to help him grow a little longer.

blocks.text: So next time you're wandering Blair Street, keep an eye out. Bring a rock, add your touch, and help Blake slither a little further. Because yes — there is a snake in Bondi. Just one. And he's the kind that makes everyone smile.

Bondi's dining goes well beyond fish and chips on the sand. There's cliff-top Italian, produce-driven fine dining that's been going since the early '90s, beachfront seafood and a new wave of share-plate spots on Hall Street. Below is the shortlist I'd steer a visitor towards — grouped by the kind of night you're after, with what each place is known for and who it suits. I write as a local curator rather than claiming to have dined at each one this month, so book ahead for the big ones and check current details before you go.

blocks.title: A living guide
blocks.text: Restaurants change — menus, chefs and hours shift, and the best tables book out. I last reviewed this in August 2026; confirm opening days and book ahead on the venue's own channels before a special trip.
Best for a special occasion
Icebergs Dining Room and Bar

Icebergs is the Bondi bucket-list dinner — a glamorous, glass-walled Italian dining room on the southern cliff, looking straight down over the Icebergs pool and the ocean. Overseen by hospitality figure Maurice Terzini, it's polished coastal Italian with one of the best views of any restaurant in Sydney. Best for: a celebration, a long lunch, or impressing visitors — book well ahead, and it's at the premium end. You can pair it with a look at the [Icebergs pool and where to swim](/where-to-swim-at-bondi-beach) below.
Sean's (formerly Sean's Panorama)

A genuine Bondi institution: chef Sean Moran has run this small, produce-led restaurant on Campbell Parade since 1993 (now simply "Sean's"). The short, hand-written menu changes with what's good, much of it from the chef's own farm. It's understated and beloved rather than flashy. Best for: a considered, ingredient-first dinner or weekend lunch — a small room, so booking is wise.
Beachfront seafood
North Bondi Fish

About as beachfront as dining gets — right on Ramsgate Avenue at the north end, with the sand almost at the door. The menu is easy-going seafood: sashimi, calamari, tacos, and fish and chips, plus cocktails. Best for: a relaxed lunch or early dinner with a view, and a solid choice with kids in tow.
Fish Shop

A casual, nautical-themed seafood spot a short walk back from the beach — the more laid-back, everyday alternative to a big seafood night out. Best for: an unfussy seafood feed without a special-occasion price tag.
Italian & share plates
Totti's Bondi

Totti's, behind The Royal on Bondi Road, is the crowd-pleasing Italian everyone seems to end up at — famous for its pillowy wood-fired bread and generous, family-style plates in a sunny, convivial room. Best for: a group, a birthday, or a long boozy lunch — it's popular, so book ahead.
Newer and something different
LULU

One of the newer names worth knowing, LULU is a funky Pan-Asian bar and kitchen on Hall Street built around share plates — think Vietnamese-style prawn banh mi, Korean fried chicken and fresh sashimi, with drinks to match. Best for: a livelier, share-and-graze dinner away from the beachfront. (As a newer venue, check its days and hours before you rely on it.)
What's changed recently

A couple of things to note for 2026. Hall Street has picked up newer, more casual share-plate venues like LULU, which are worth a look alongside the classics. Sean's Panorama now trades simply as "Sean's" — same chef, same Campbell Parade address, so don't be thrown by the shorter name. And the refurbished Bondi Pavilion has reopened on the beachfront with its food and drink line-up reshuffled since the works, so check who's trading there now rather than trusting older guides.
What to know before you go

items: Book ahead for the big ones: Icebergs, Totti's and Sean's fill up, especially for weekend lunch and warm evenings.
Timing: sunset tables with a view (Icebergs, North Bondi Fish) are the most sought-after — reserve early or aim for lunch.
Price: Icebergs and Sean's sit at the premium end; North Bondi Fish, Fish Shop and LULU are more mid-range.
Getting there: it's an easy night out on foot or by bus — see [getting to Bondi](/getting-to-bondi) if you're coming from the city.
Make a day of it: line up a swim or the coastal walk first — see [things to do in Bondi](/things-to-do-in-bondi).

blocks.text: Which Bondi restaurant is right for you?

items: Special occasion with a view: Icebergs Dining Room and Bar.
Ingredient-led, understated dinner: Sean's (Campbell Parade).
Beachfront seafood: North Bondi Fish.
Casual, everyday seafood: Fish Shop.
Group Italian / long lunch: Totti's Bondi.
Livelier newer share plates: LULU (Hall Street).

items.q: What is the best restaurant in Bondi?
items.a: For a special-occasion dinner with a view, Icebergs Dining Room and Bar is the classic pick. For understated, produce-driven cooking, Sean's on Campbell Parade has been a favourite since 1993.

items.q: Where can I eat right on Bondi Beach?
items.a: North Bondi Fish is the most beachfront option, on Ramsgate Avenue at the north end. Icebergs sits above the pool on the southern cliff with the best elevated view.

items.q: Which Bondi restaurant has the best view?
items.a: Icebergs Dining Room and Bar, looking over the Icebergs pool and the ocean, is hard to beat; North Bondi Fish gets you closest to the sand.

items.q: Are there any newer restaurants in Bondi?
items.a: Yes — Hall Street has picked up newer share-plate spots such as LULU, a Pan-Asian bar and kitchen. Note that Sean's Panorama now trades simply as "Sean's".

items.q: Do I need to book a Bondi restaurant?
items.a: For Icebergs, Totti's and Sean's, yes — book ahead, especially for weekend lunch and warm evenings. Casual spots like Fish Shop and North Bondi Fish are more forgiving.

blocks.text: Bondi packs one of Sydney's best café scenes into a few walkable streets behind the beach — beachfront brunch rooms, serious coffee windows, and a run of newer openings worth knowing about in 2026. Below is the shortlist I'd hand a visitor: what each place is known for, roughly where it is, and who it suits. I write these as a local curator rather than claiming to have eaten at every one this week, so treat the details as a well-researched starting point and check current hours before a special trip.

blocks.title: A living guide
blocks.text: Bondi's café scene moves fast — hours, menus and even owners change. I last reviewed this in August 2026; confirm anything time-sensitive on the venue's own channels before you go.
Best beachfront cafés for brunch
Speedos Café — North Bondi

Speedos sits up at the quieter North Bondi end (Ramsgate Avenue) with some of the best ocean views of any café on the beach. It's the classic post-swim spot — health-leaning brunch, bowls, pancakes and juices, with window benches looking straight out to the water. Best for: a relaxed, view-first breakfast at the north end.
Chapter One — Campbell Parade

Right on Campbell Parade opposite the sand, Chapter One is a café-meets-wine-bar that's been going since 2012, pouring Allpress coffee alongside an all-day menu. It's an easy, central choice if you want to be directly across from the beach. Best for: an all-rounder in the middle of the action.
bills — Hall Street

The Sydney institution founded by Bill Granger has been on Hall Street (number 79) since 2014, and it's still open and busy. Come for the dishes that made it famous — ricotta hotcakes and sweetcorn fritters — in a light, airy room. Best for: a benchmark Bondi brunch and a bit of Sydney food history.
Best for specialty coffee
Harry's Bondi — Wairoa Avenue

Harry's has been caffeinating Bondi since 1997 and is my pick if coffee is the point. It grew from a hole-in-the-wall into a full café, with batch brew, espresso and cold drip plus a following for its matcha and specialty lattes. Best for: coffee-first locals and a quick, quality cup.
Sonoma — bakery coffee

Sonoma is the well-known Sydney sourdough bakery with a Bondi outpost — a reliable stop for a proper coffee and a pastry or bakery-driven breakfast without the full brunch sit-down. Best for: a quick, high-quality grab-and-go.
Gertrude & Alice — Hall Street

Genuinely one of a kind: a second-hand bookshop and café on Hall Street where you can settle in with Campos coffee, a Middle Eastern-leaning breakfast and a stack of books. It's the antidote to Bondi's see-and-be-seen rooms. Best for: a slow, quiet morning and something different.
Strong all-rounders just back from the sand
Blackwood — Glenayr Avenue

An Eastern Suburbs brunch staple a couple of streets back, Blackwood is known for a seasonal menu that blends Mediterranean and Asian influences — ricotta pancakes, chilli scrambled eggs — with carefully made coffee. Best for: a considered brunch away from the beachfront crush.
Porch and Parlour — North Bondi

A long-running North Bondi favourite (Ramsgate Avenue) built around local produce, with its well-known pea pancakes and a reliably buzzy weekend. It's also one of the better-known dog-friendly spots. Best for: a neighbourhood brunch with the dog in tow.
Newer and more unusual spots
Cafe Bondi — North Bondi (new)

One of the more recent openings, Cafe Bondi is on Campbell Parade at the North Bondi end and opens early for coffee, sunshine and an easy all-day menu. Best for: an early start at the quieter north end. (As a newer venue, double-check its days and hours before you rely on it.)
Up South — Bondi Road

Further up Bondi Road, Up South made its name on playful matcha creations and a rotating treats cabinet — the spot for a strawberry or pistachio matcha and a photo. Best for: matcha fans and a sweet mid-morning stop.
Lox, Stock & Barrel — bagels & deli
A Bondi take on a Jewish deli, known for artisan bagels and generous, deli-influenced brunch plates. Best for: a bagel-led breakfast or an easy weekday lunch.
Makaveli & Pocket — café by day, bar by night

From the same team, Makaveli (Glenayr Avenue) and Pocket (Campbell Parade) both work the café-to-cocktail-bar angle — pastries, loaded sourdough and coffee in the morning, share plates and drinks later. Best for: a laid-back start that can roll into the afternoon.
What's changed recently

Two things worth flagging for 2026. First, there's genuine new blood at the north end — Cafe Bondi being the clearest recent opening. Second, the former Hall Street all-day spot Bondi Hall has closed, so ignore older lists that still feature it. The refurbished Bondi Pavilion has also reopened with food and drink operators on the beachfront; those line-ups have shifted since the works, so check who's trading there now rather than trusting an older guide.
What to know before you go

items: Timing: arrive close to opening or after about 2pm to dodge the worst queues; weekend mornings are the busiest.
Booking: most Bondi cafés are walk-in, though a few take reservations for larger groups — check ahead if there are more than four of you.
Dogs: several are dog-friendly, with Porch and Parlour the best-known; outdoor tables are your friend.
Reusables: bring a keep-cup — some cafés knock a little off for it.
Make a morning of it: pair a café with the Saturday [Bondi Farmers Market](/whats-on/markets), or a swim first — see [where to swim at Bondi](/where-to-swim-at-bondi-beach).

blocks.text: Which Bondi café is right for you?

items: Best ocean view: Speedos Café (North Bondi).
Best coffee: Harry's Bondi (serving since 1997).
Most iconic brunch: bills (Hall Street).
Something different: Gertrude & Alice (bookshop café, Hall Street).
Newest: Cafe Bondi (North Bondi).
Best with a dog: Porch and Parlour (North Bondi).

items.q: What is the best café in Bondi?
items.a: It depends what you want. For a beachfront brunch with a view I'd point you to Speedos Café or Chapter One; for the best coffee, Harry's Bondi; and for an iconic Sydney breakfast, bills on Hall Street.

items.q: Which Bondi café has the best view?
items.a: Speedos Café at North Bondi and Chapter One on Campbell Parade both look straight out over the beach — the two I'd choose for a view-first breakfast.

items.q: Where is the best coffee in Bondi?
items.a: Harry's Bondi has been a coffee benchmark since 1997. Sonoma is a reliable bakery-coffee stop, and Gertrude & Alice pours Campos in a bookshop setting.

items.q: Are there any new cafés in Bondi?
items.a: Cafe Bondi at the North Bondi end is one of the clearer recent openings. Note that the older Hall Street spot Bondi Hall has closed, so skip it on out-of-date lists.

items.q: Do I need to book a Bondi café?
items.a: Most are walk-in. Expect queues on weekend mornings, so arrive early or after about 2pm, and check ahead only if you're a larger group.

items.q: Are there dog-friendly cafés in Bondi?
items.a: Yes — Porch and Parlour in North Bondi is the best-known dog-friendly option, and many cafés welcome dogs at their outdoor tables.

blocks.text: However you play it, Bondi rewards a bit of café-hopping — a coffee at the north end, a swim, then brunch on Campbell Parade. For more on eating and drinking around the beach, see my [Bondi eat & drink guide](/bondi-eat-and-drink); for the rest of a day here, [things to do in Bondi](/things-to-do-in-bondi); and for markets and events, [what's on in Bondi](/whats-on).

blocks.text: The City2Surf draws tens of thousands of runners every August for its atmosphere, its city-to-sea course, and one very famous hill. Whether it's your first or you're chasing a personal best, a bit of preparation goes a long way. Here are the ten things I'd tell any mate before they line up.
1. Know the course

It's 14 km from the CBD to Bondi. The opening kilometres are fast and net downhill, then around the middle you hit Heartbreak Hill — roughly a 2 km climb from Rose Bay to Vaucluse. Knowing where the hill sits helps you save energy for it instead of blowing up early.
2. Enter early and pick the right wave

Entries open earlier in the year and sell out — the 2026 event sold out well before race day. Register as soon as entries open, and choose a start wave that matches your realistic finish time so you're not weaving through slower runners (or holding up faster ones).
3. Train for the hill

Heartbreak Hill is what people remember. Add hill repeats to your training once a week in the lead-up so both your legs and your head know what a sustained climb feels like. It's the single best thing you can do for your time.
4. Build up gradually

Increase your weekly distance slowly rather than cramming. A mix of one longer run, some faster efforts and easy recovery jogs beats a couple of heroic long runs. Consistency is what gets you to 14 km comfortably.
5. Sort your hydration and fuelling

Hydrate in the days before, not just on the morning. Have a light, familiar breakfast a couple of hours before the start. Whatever gels or drinks you plan to use, practise with them in training first.
6. Gear you've tested — and sunscreen

Wear well-broken-in shoes and light, moisture-wicking clothing. Nothing brand new on race day. And even in August, put on sweat-resistant sunscreen before the start — the sun really shows up by the time you reach Bondi.
7. Plan your transport

Roads close and the nearest stations fill early. Give yourself a solid hour of buffer to get to the start, find the gear check, queue for the loo and warm up. Public transport beats driving every time on race day.
8. Check the weather

Early-August Sydney can swing from cool and grey to surprisingly warm. Check the Bureau of Meteorology forecast and dress accordingly — a cheap layer you can shed at the start line is a good friend on a cold morning.
9. Pace it in thirds

Start conservatively, run the hill on effort rather than staring at your pace, and use the downhills to recover without over-striding. Break the run into thirds and reassess how you feel at each. Negative-splitting the City2Surf feels a lot better than fading.
10. Recover and celebrate

Keep walking for a few minutes after the line rather than stopping dead, grab water and a snack, and agree a meeting spot with your crew in advance — phone signal gets patchy in the crowd. Then reward yourself: brunch, a swim, or a dip at the Icebergs pool. You've earned it.

items.q: How long is the City2Surf and how hilly is it?
items.a: 14 km, and hillier than first-timers expect. The main climb is Heartbreak Hill, about 2 km from Rose Bay to Vaucluse near halfway, with a few more short rises after it.

items.q: Do City2Surf entries sell out?
items.a: Yes — it's very popular and sells out ahead of race day, so enter early through city2surf.com.au and pick a start wave matching your expected finish time.

items.q: What should I not do on race day?
items.a: Don't wear or eat anything you haven't tested in training, don't go out too fast, and don't skip sunscreen — the Sydney sun is strong by the Bondi finish.

blocks.text: The lifeguards you know from Bondi Rescue are real professional lifeguards employed by Waverley Council, not actors — the same crew in blue and yellow who patrol Bondi Beach every day of the year. The TV show made them household names, but their day job is keeping one of the world's busiest beaches safe. Here's who the best-known lifeguards are, some facts about the show, and how to see the team in action. The roster changes over the seasons, so I keep this updated as things shift.

blocks.title: A note I keep current
blocks.text: Lifeguard line-ups rotate and some faces move on, so treat the bios below as the well-known regulars rather than a live roster. I last reviewed this in August 2026.
What is Bondi Rescue?

Bondi Rescue is the documentary series that follows the Waverley Council lifeguards through the Australian summer. It first aired in 2006 on Network 10, is made by production company CJZ, and has run for around 18 seasons — one of Australia's longest-running and most-exported factual shows, screening in dozens of countries. It was rested in 2025 (no new season that year) and, according to its producers, is expected to return, with filming subject to arrangements with Waverley Council. Either way, the lifeguards themselves keep patrolling Bondi.
The Bondi lifeguards you'll recognise
Bruce ‘Hoppo’ Hopkins — head lifeguard

Hoppo is the head lifeguard and the show's steady centre of gravity. He's been part of the Bondi lifeguard service since the early 1990s, and on screen he's the calm, experienced voice coordinating the team through busy days and serious rescues. If there's one name people associate with Bondi Rescue, it's his.
Anthony ‘Harries’ Carroll

Harries is one of the show's most recognisable and charismatic lifeguards — high-energy, endlessly committed on a rescue, and known for his fundraising and community antics off the sand. He's one of the longest-serving faces of the team.
Andrew ‘Reidy’ Reid
Reidy is a seasoned member of the crew, known on the show for his humour and his fitness, with a strong social-media following. He's one of the regulars viewers have followed across many seasons.
Trent ‘Maxi’ Maxwell

Maxi came through as one of the younger lifeguards and became a fan favourite. He's also widely known for working as a firefighter — splitting his time between saving lives on the beach and in the city.
Dean ‘Deano’ Gladstone
Deano is another long-serving member of the team who's featured across many seasons of the show.

Plenty of other lifeguards have featured over the years — you'll hear nicknames like Jesse, Chappo, Whippet, Yatesy, Mouse and Kobi among them. Because the team rotates season to season, I focus above on the best-known regulars rather than trying to list everyone currently rostered.
Interesting facts about Bondi Rescue

items: The lifeguards are real Waverley Council employees — professional, paid lifeguards, not actors and not the same thing as the volunteer surf lifesavers in the red-and-yellow caps.
Bondi is one of the most rescue-heavy beaches in Australia, largely thanks to a notorious rip at the south end nicknamed the ‘Backpackers' Express’.
The show is filmed across the Australian summer, when Bondi's crowds — and the number of rescues — peak.
Bondi Rescue has been sold to dozens of countries, making Bondi's lifeguards internationally famous.

For the full run-down, see our companion pieces on [20 obscure facts about Bondi Rescue](/bondi-blog/2023/9/5/20-obscure-facts-about-bondi-rescue) and [the most dramatic moments on the show](/bondi-blog/2025/1/12/the-20-most-dramatic-moments-on-bondi-rescue).

blocks.text: Key moments from the show

Across its seasons Bondi Rescue has captured everything from huge multi-swimmer rescues on wild-surf days to tense resuscitations, shark alarms clearing the water, and the occasional celebrity spotting on the sand. Rather than rank them here, I've pulled the standouts together in a dedicated guide — see [the 20 most dramatic moments on Bondi Rescue](/bondi-blog/2025/1/12/the-20-most-dramatic-moments-on-bondi-rescue).
Can you meet the Bondi lifeguards?

Yes — the lifeguards are on Bondi Beach every day, based around the lifeguard tower towards the south end near the flags. You'll often see the Bondi Rescue crew there in season. A few things I'd keep in mind: they're working, and their first job is watching the water, so give them space during busy periods and never interrupt a rescue for a photo. Swim between the red-and-yellow flags and you're in the patch they're actively watching. The team also has official merchandise and an active social presence if you want to follow along.

blocks.title: Swim between the flags
blocks.text: The best way to respect the lifeguards' work is simple: always swim between the red-and-yellow flags, where they've judged it safest and are watching. See our guide to [where to swim at Bondi](/where-to-swim-at-bondi-beach) for the safest spots.

items.q: Are the Bondi Rescue lifeguards real?
items.a: Yes. They're real professional lifeguards employed by Waverley Council who patrol Bondi Beach year-round. The show is a documentary series, not scripted drama, and the rescues are real.

items.q: Who is the head lifeguard at Bondi?
items.a: Bruce ‘Hoppo’ Hopkins is the long-serving head lifeguard and the most recognisable figure from the show, part of the Bondi service since the early 1990s.

items.q: Is Bondi Rescue still on?
items.a: The show was rested in 2025 with no new season that year, but its producers have said it's expected to return, subject to arrangements with Waverley Council. The lifeguards continue to patrol Bondi regardless.

items.q: Are Bondi lifeguards the same as surf lifesavers?
items.a: No. The Bondi Rescue lifeguards are paid, professional council lifeguards. Volunteer surf lifesavers (in the red-and-yellow caps) are a separate service that also patrols, typically on weekends and public holidays.

items.q: Can I meet the Bondi Rescue lifeguards?
items.a: You can usually see the team around the lifeguard tower on Bondi Beach in season. Be respectful — they're working and watching the water — and never interrupt a rescue.

blocks.text: However you know them — from the tower or the TV — Bondi's lifeguards are a huge part of what makes the beach what it is. For more, see the [Bondi Rescue hub](/bondi-rescue), our guide to [where to swim safely at Bondi](/where-to-swim-at-bondi-beach), and the rest of [things to do in Bondi](/things-to-do-in-bondi).

blocks.text: I hear it mangled at least once a day down at the beach, usually from a visitor asking directions. So let me settle it for you: Bondi is said "BON-dye" — the last bit rhymes with "eye", not "ee".

For Australians who grew up with Bondi, there's no question about it — but the spelling trips up overseas visitors, who very reasonably read the "i" on the end as "ee". It isn't. Think "bond" (like a secret agent) followed by "eye", with the emphasis on that first syllable: BON-dye.
What "Bondi" actually means

The name is Aboriginal. Waverley Council, which looks after the beach, records that Bondi comes from a local Aboriginal word meaning "the sound of the waves breaking on the beach" (you'll also see it given as "water breaking over rocks"). Once you know that, the name makes perfect sense — stand on the promenade for a minute and the meaning is all around you.
Easy way to lock it in: it rhymes with "Aussie hi" — Bon-dye, not Bon-dee. Get the ending right and you'll sound like you've been coming here for years.

items.q: How do you pronounce Bondi?
items.a: "BON-dye" — "bond" followed by "eye", with the stress on the first syllable. The "i" at the end sounds like "eye", not "ee".

items.q: Is it BON-dee or BON-dye?
items.a: BON-dye. "BON-dee" is the most common mispronunciation among overseas visitors, but locals say BON-dye.

items.q: What does Bondi mean?
items.a: It's from a local Aboriginal word. Waverley Council records the meaning as "the sound of the waves breaking on the beach" (also commonly translated as "water breaking over rocks").

blocks.text: Hope that helps — now say it with confidence and enjoy the beach.

blocks.text: Every August, my end of Sydney turns into a finish line. The City2Surf is the run that ends at Bondi, and whether I'm out on the course or cheering from the promenade, it's one of my favourite days of the year. Here's my local guide to running it well — and enjoying it.

The City2Surf is one of the world's largest fun runs — tens of thousands of people, from elite racers to first-timers in fancy dress, all making the 14 km journey from the city to the sea. It starts near Hyde Park in the CBD (at Park and College Streets) and finishes on the grass above Bondi Beach. Part race, part street party, it's Sydney at its most joyful.
The route — and yes, Heartbreak Hill

From the start you drop down William Street, through the Kings Cross tunnel, then out along New South Head Road with the harbour glinting beside you through Rose Bay. Then comes the bit everyone's heard about: Heartbreak Hill, a roughly 2 km climb from Rose Bay up to Vaucluse. It's the halfway point and the make-or-break section. From Vaucluse you head along Old South Head Road and Military Road before a glorious downhill toward the coast, a turnaround near Curlewis Street, and the finish on Queen Elizabeth Drive at Bondi.

blocks.title: Two things first-timers don't expect
blocks.text: Heartbreak Hill isn't the end of the climbing — there are several short, sharp pinches after it, so keep something in reserve. And don't empty the tank on the final downhill: after you reach the bottom there's still around a kilometre of flat, switchback running to the line. Save a little for it.
Getting there and home

Public transport is by far the easiest option — roads close across the eastern suburbs and parking near the start or finish is a nightmare. Bring an Opal card or tap on with a card or phone. For the start, trains to St James, Museum or Town Hall put you a short walk from the assembly area. Getting home from Bondi, there are usually free shuttle buses to Bondi Junction where you can pick up the T4 line back to the city. Because the exact shuttle and closure details change each year, I check Transport for NSW's event page in the days before.
My tips for a strong run

items: Train on hills. Even a few weeks of hill repeats makes Heartbreak Hill far less scary.
Go out easy. Aim to run the second half faster than the first — the crowd energy will tempt you to sprint the opening kilometres; don't.
On the hill, shorten your stride and hold a steady effort. People who charge past you early are usually the ones walking it near the top.
Don't experiment on race day — no new shoes, gear or energy gels you haven't tried in training.
At water stations, keep moving through rather than stopping dead; it keeps you and everyone behind you safe.
Sunscreen and a cap. It's August, but the Sydney sun still bites by the time you reach Bondi.

blocks.text: The finish (and the afterparty)

Crossing the line above Bondi Beach, salt air in your lungs and the ocean right there, never gets old. Once you've caught your breath, the celebrating begins — the Bondi pubs and the Pavilion turn on afterparties every year. I've written a separate guide to the best spots to recover and celebrate, and a companion piece on the things I wish I'd known before my first City2Surf.

items.q: How long is the City2Surf?
items.a: 14 kilometres, from Sydney's CBD (near Hyde Park) to the finish above Bondi Beach.

items.q: When is City2Surf 2026?
items.a: Sunday 9 August 2026. The 2026 event is sold out — for entries and future dates, check the official site at city2surf.com.au.

items.q: Where is Heartbreak Hill?
items.a: It's an approximately 2 km climb along New South Head Road from Rose Bay up to Vaucluse, at roughly the halfway mark of the course.

items.q: How do I get to the start and back from Bondi?
items.a: Use public transport — roads close and parking is very limited. Trains reach the CBD start; from the Bondi finish there are usually free shuttles to Bondi Junction for the train home. Check Transport for NSW for the current year's details.

blocks.text: Whether you're chasing a personal best or just want to say you've run from the city to the surf, City2Surf is a Sydney rite of passage. Train a little, pace it smart, and I'll see you at the Bondi end.

blocks.text: I'll be honest: parking at Bondi on a sunny weekend can test your patience like nothing else. But after years of doing it, I've got a system. Here's where I actually park, from free spots to the paid stations, and the tricks I use on the busiest days.

blocks.title: Read the signs
blocks.text: Parking inspectors patrol Bondi constantly and the fines are steep — and never block a driveway (that's around a $500 penalty). Always check the sign for time limits and permit zones before you walk off.
Free parking

My go-to: the residential streets north of Blair Street, away from the beach. It's free and unrestricted 24 hours, and it's about a 5–7 minute walk down to the sand. On weekdays it's easy until around 6pm when residents get home; on weekends it fills through the morning, so get in early.
Paid parking

items: Bondi Beach Parking Station (Queen Elizabeth Drive) — the closest and largest, right behind the beach. It fills fast on a nice day, so arrive early.
Pacific Bondi car park — directly opposite the Bondi Pavilion, a two-minute walk to the sand, open long hours daily. Booking online is usually cheaper than driving up.
Wilson Parking at The Hub (Hall Street) — often overlooked; pricey, but a solid option for an hour or two on a hectic day.
Street meters near the shops and along the beachfront — handy but the priciest per hour, and time-limited.

blocks.text: A tip that's saved me plenty: use a parking app like Parkopedia or the operators' own apps to see availability and pre-book a bay before you leave home.

blocks.title: What does it cost?
blocks.text: Beachfront and beach-adjacent meters are the dearest — recently in the order of $7–11 per hour depending on the zone and the season — and they get cheaper the further back from the sand you go. Council adjusts these rates periodically, so check Waverley Council's current parking meter fees rather than trusting a fixed figure (including mine).
Where I park on the really busy days

items: South Bondi — around Edward Street, Francis Street and the surrounding blocks. Most people head for the middle of the beach, so these can be surprisingly lucky.
Around the Beach Road Hotel — always busy, but it doesn't pull the beach crowd the way the streets closer to the sand do.
North of Blair Street — North Bondi is the hardest area to park, but once you're past Blair Street heading away from the beach, spots open up (and they're free).

items.q: Is there free parking at Bondi Beach?
items.a: Yes — the residential streets north of Blair Street are free and unrestricted 24 hours, about a 5–7 minute walk to the beach. Get there early on weekends.

items.q: How much does it cost to park at Bondi Beach?
items.a: Beach-adjacent meters and the Queen Elizabeth Drive station are the priciest (recently roughly $7–11 per hour depending on zone and season). Rates change, so check Waverley Council for the current figure.

items.q: What's the closest car park to Bondi Beach?
items.a: The Bondi Beach Parking Station on Queen Elizabeth Drive, right behind the sand. It fills quickly on sunny days, so arrive early.

blocks.text: My honest advice? On a perfect summer's day, skip the parking lottery altogether and catch the train to Bondi Junction then the bus down — you'll be on the sand while everyone else is still circling the block.

blocks.text: You've survived the 14 km from the city to the sea — now for the best part. The Bondi afterparty is a City2Surf tradition, and as a local I can tell you the whole beachfront turns into one big celebration the moment the runners start pouring in. Here's where I'd point you.

blocks.title: Get in early
blocks.text: Every good spot fills fast as tens of thousands of people flood into Bondi. By midday you're looking at long queues, so head straight from the finish to your chosen venue — or, if you're just here for the party, aim to be in place by around 11am. The specific line-ups, DJ sets and drink deals change every year, so check each venue's own socials for what they've got on this time.
The reliable Bondi afterparty spots
Hotel Ravesis

The long-standing go-to for runners and their support crew, right on the corner overlooking the beach. Those balcony tables are gold and go early — it's a short dash from the finish, so don't stop running just yet.
Royal Bondi
A Merivale venue that reliably throws one of the bigger, livelier parties, with DJs and a buzzing crowd. Always a safe bet for atmosphere.
Beach Road Hotel

"The Beachy" is a Bondi institution and often hosts the biggest afterparty of the lot. It's a little further from the finish, so it rewards those with legs left in them — and be warned, the queue can be the biggest too.
North Bondi Fish & North Bondi RSL

Up the quieter northern end of the beach, these two are my pick for views and a slightly more relaxed vibe. North Bondi Fish does the beachfront-dining thing with DJs and ocean views; the RSL next door is simply one of the best-value, most easygoing spots on Bondi for a post-race beer.
Hotel Bondi & the Bondi Pavilion

If your legs have completely seized up, Hotel Bondi sits close to the finish and is always lively. The Bondi Pavilion, right on the sand, also regularly hosts finish-line celebrations — worth a look for something a bit different.

items.q: Where's the best City2Surf afterparty in Bondi?
items.a: The perennial favourites are Hotel Ravesis and Royal Bondi near the finish, and the Beach Road Hotel a little further on for the biggest party. North Bondi RSL and North Bondi Fish are great for a more relaxed celebration with a view.

items.q: What time should I get there?
items.a: As early as you can — venues fill and queues build by midday. Head straight from the finish, or be in place by around 11am if you're just coming for the party.

items.q: How do I find out this year's events and deals?
items.a: Line-ups, DJs and drink specials change each year. Check each venue's own social media, or the official City2Surf channels, for the current year's finish-line events.

blocks.text: However you celebrate, pace the day like you paced the run — plenty of water between drinks, and soak up that unbeatable Bondi finish-line feeling. You earned it.

blocks.text: A day at Bondi isn't complete without getting in the water — and you've really got three choices: the beach itself, the famous Icebergs ocean pool, or the calm little kids' pool at North Bondi. Here's how I'd pick, and how to do it safely.
Swimming on the beach

The beach is free and open to everyone, and Bondi is patrolled by professional lifeguards year-round. The single most important rule: always swim between the red-and-yellow flags, where the lifeguards have judged it safest and are watching. The northern end of the beach is usually the more sheltered, calmer spot — my pick for a relaxed dip and for families. The southern end tends to be for stronger swimmers and surfers, and it's where the beach's notorious rip (the "Backpackers' Express") runs, so it's not the place to wade in if you're unsure.

blocks.title: Read the water first
blocks.text: Bondi has rips that can pull even confident swimmers out fast. Swim between the flags, never swim alone or after drinking, and if you're caught in a rip stay calm, raise an arm and float — don't fight it. Check Beachsafe for the day's conditions before you go in.
Bondi Icebergs ocean pool

The Icebergs is the postcard — a 50-metre ocean pool cut into the rocks at the southern headland, filled and refreshed by the sea, with a shallower pool beside it for little ones. The public is welcome (it's not members-only), there's a sauna to thaw out in winter, and the Crabbe Hole café is a lovely spot for a coffee afterwards. One thing to know: the pool sits right on the ocean, so it closes for cleaning and when big swells or repairs are needed — check the Icebergs website for current opening hours before you make a special trip.
The kids' pool at North Bondi

If you've got young children, head to the north end. The little sandy-bottomed children's pool there (the Wally Weekes pool) is shallow, calm and sheltered — by far the most relaxed place at Bondi to let small kids splash without the waves.
Rock pools, and swims nearby

At low tide you'll find rock pools along the edges of the beach worth exploring. And if you're up for a short walk, the coastal path south leads to Bronte and its own free ocean baths — one of my favourite swims in the whole city.
A lap swim, rain or shine
If you just want to do laps regardless of the surf or the weather, there's an indoor pool a short distance from the beach — handy on a grey day or when the ocean's too rough.

items.q: Can the public swim at Bondi Icebergs?
items.a: Yes — Bondi Icebergs is open to the public, not just members. There's a small entry fee, a 50m lap pool and a shallow kids' pool. Check the Icebergs website for current hours, as it closes for cleaning and big swells.

items.q: Where is the calmest place to swim at Bondi?
items.a: The northern end of the beach and the shallow children's pool at North Bondi are the calmest, most sheltered spots — ideal for families and less confident swimmers.

items.q: Where should I swim if I have young kids?
items.a: The kids' pool at North Bondi (the Wally Weekes pool) is shallow and calm. On the beach, stay at the north end and always between the flags.

items.q: Is it safe to swim at Bondi Beach?
items.a: Bondi is patrolled by lifeguards daily, but the ocean always carries risk. Swim between the red-and-yellow flags, check conditions on Beachsafe, don't swim alone, and never underestimate the rips — especially at the southern end.

blocks.text: However you like your swim — a bracing lap in the Icebergs, a gentle float at the north end, or riding the shore break — Bondi has a spot for it. Just read the water, swim between the flags, and you'll have the swim of the trip.
